doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

chapter: Tuba in jazz history and technique
title: Early tuba players, two-beat music and the tuba's decline
summary: After an audio example, they discuss early tuba thinking, two-beat feel, and tuba players such as Major Holley, Pops Foster and Red Callender.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: And I was listening to, in fact I’m going to put on a little piece of something here. Let’s see if I can push the right button.

Now I’m not sure that we can put ourselves in the mind of that tuba player, but this was sort of new ground at the times I guess, or jazz was sort of forming. Do you know, how would that person be thinking, okay I’ve got to play the root then fifth?
And do you think they have — I don’t even know how to phrase this question — but do would they be thinking this is two-beat music?
I’m not sure whether they would be thinking two-beat music because that was the music that was being played at the time. It wasn’t like there was some other music. There © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

wasn’t a four-beat at the time. You know, so they wouldn’t necessarily be thinking well am I going to go [scats] or [scats]. He’d probably just do what he was doing. He wouldn’t necessarily just think of it as two-beat because at that time there was no music going [scats]. So he might not be thinking about four particularly, unless they did a stop chorus where they went [scats]. And they wouldn’t necessarily think in four they’d just say it’s a stop chorus of they’d do one of those [scats] or play three notes or play two notes or whatever they chose to do.
Why was the — you know you said in your recent CD here that the tuba kind of went out of favor, late twenties?

Late twenties and the beginnings of the swing era, beginnings when the bands started to get really larger, the big band kind of things. Still some big bands held on to a tuba player that doubled on bass like many bass players that came through that period — Slam Stewart, Major Holly, a lot of them played tuba. Major Holly was a great tuba player.
You even have a picture of Pops Foster.
Right. Red Callender was a great tuba —

Yeah he was a great tuba player. Yeah. I mean he was playing with Lester Young all through most of the forties and during — you see him in movies with Louis Armstrong in the background of one of those movies where he’s wearing this straw hat, you know, one of those flat brim hats. But he was a great tuba player.
